children: Shares of Solstice Advanced Materials soared early Friday after the company called off a dramatic acquisition that would have turned the company into even more of an AI play.

In early July, Solstice announced a cash and stock deal to buy Element Solutions. Element makes products used in semiconductor manufacturing. Solstice produces refrigerants as well as uranium hexafluoride, an intermediate product in the process of making nuclear reactor fuel. Together, the companies would supply three legs of the AI value chain: The chips, the data centers, and the power that makes everything work.

It was a significant step for Solstice, which recently spun out of Honeywell Technologies, essentially doubling its size. Investors didn't like the deal, though. Solstice stock was trading above $80 before the announcement. It was below $57 heading into Friday trading. Element stock was north of $42 before the announcement. It closed on Thursday at $36.52.
Stock performance might be one reason why the deal was called off. Investors might have also worried about added debt or the ability of a new company to integrate a large, different business.

"Following conversations with our shareholders and discussions between the parties, both Boards unanimously believe that it is in the best interests of our respective shareholders, employees and customers to terminate the merger agreement," said Rajeev Gautam, chairman of the Solstice board of directors, in a news release.

"Initially, we were positive on the... deal as we thought the Solstice sell-off (greater than 20%) post-announcement was somewhat overblown," wrote RBC analyst Arun Viswanathan on Friday. He thought the price paid, about 21 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, was attractive, noting peers trade for 25 to 30 times.
"That said, given the strong negative response and subsequent deal cancellation, we applaud Solstice management's return to its initial strategy to pursue significant organic [growth]," he wrote.

That sentiment was echoed on the Street. UBS analyst Joshua Spector called the decision a positive for both stocks. And BMO analyst John McNulty said Solstice is an "undervalued and compelling way to invest in the high-growth Uranium/ electronics/refrig markets."
Those are three fundamental analysts that rate Solstice stock Buy. Gordon Haskett analyst Don Bilson doesn't cover Solstice. His expertise is in special situations, including deals.

"We've been skeptical that Element Solutions's management team could deliver the [shareholder] votes needed, and rather than drag their respective shareholder bases through a meat-grinder, the two companies wisely decided to let this one go," wrote Bilson on Friday.

The Street backs the decision to abandon the deal. "While we viewed the Element acquisition as an opportunity to accelerate our strategy, we have great confidence in our strategic plan and respect our shareholders' views," said CEO David Sewell.
His company also announced a $500 million share repurchase. Shares were up 16% in midday trading on Friday at $65.33, while the S&P 500 was up 0.4%. Element stock was up 0.2%.
Investors wanted both companies to remain separate. They got what they wanted. Time will tell if that was the best outcome for both.
